title: A hymn in Jaijavanti
hook: it's passing, it's passing: Guru Tegh Bahadur talks to the mind about time, and the week looks back

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Jaijavanti, where the ragas end and Guru Tegh Bahadur sings alone. Your line was the last raga. What were you building, and what is it made of? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven.

Departing. Departing. On a station board the word blinks beside a train that hasn't moved yet. The doors are still open. People are still walking, not running. The word isn't a disaster; it's information, said twice so nobody misses it. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a hymn in Jaijavanti that opens the same way, with one word said twice. It's passing. It's passing. It's this week's last day, so we'll look back over the ragas we've walked through. But first, the board, and the doors still open.
screen: `DEPARTING. DEPARTING.` → `THE DOORS ARE STILL OPEN.` → `ONE WORD, SAID TWICE.`

segments.voice: The hymns in Jaijavanti keep speaking to the mind directly. One asks it: O mind, what will become of you? And this one opens, in paraphrase: it is passing, it is passing, your life is passing to no purpose. Day and night you hear holy stories, and still you don't take them in: the same charge Parmanand made in Sarang. The time has come; where will you run? The body you counted on as steady will turn to dust. Why not remember the Name of the Lord? In Gurmukhi the opening is beet jaihai, beet jaihai, and the doubling does what the station board does. It isn't shouting. It's making sure. Notice what the hymn is not. It's blunt, even calling the mind a fool, but it isn't despair. It names time honestly, and then, in the same breath, it points to what can still be done: remember. The doors are open. That's why today's line isn't 'too late' but before it slips by. Yesterday's hymn said remembering is your work. Today's says the work has a clock. Now look back over this week. At the start of the week, Guru Arjan in Kanara: no enemy, no stranger. Then Kalyan in the evening: no one has found your limit, and we are your children; and the bee that comes back to the lotus again and again. Then Prabhati at dawn: the Name as the ornament you put on first, and Kabir's one light falling on every street. Then Jaijavanti, where the ragas end: remember, remember, this is your work. And today, the reason to start now. Evening, dawn and the end of the ragas, and the same Name running through all of them. Your line: before it slips by.
screen: `O MIND, WHAT WILL BECOME OF YOU?` · `IT'S PASSING, IT'S PASSING.` · `NOT A THREAT: THE DOORS ARE OPEN.` · `THE WEEK: STRANGER, CHILD, LIGHT, SAND.` · then, large: `BEFORE IT SLIPS BY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one Jaijavanti shabad, and use this minute while it's here. If you can, play Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn of beet jaihai, or another in Jaijavanti. If not, sit in the quiet. Feel this breath come in and go out. It's passing. The next one, passing too. Don't hold on, and don't hurry. Just be present for each one before it goes, the way you'd step through open doors without running. If you pray, you can remember the Name on each breath, the way the hymn asks. If you don't, let each breath be fully noticed before it slips by. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Jaijavanti. Guru Tegh Bahadur's song to the mind: it's passing, it's passing; why not remember the Name while there's time? Today's word.
Your line: before it slips by. Pick one thing you've been saving for later, a call, a thank-you, a visit, and do the first small piece of it today. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-seven.
